candidate: TWO candidates tried, both lost: B hue f0.70 e20, then C hue f0.90 e32 (much gentler). All three at g1.439
note: FIDELITY: A BEST BY FAR. B washed a great deal of detail into white and did not help the yellow. C was a deliberately gentle version of the same rule and was STILL worse than no chroma stage at all - white still washing, and the colour on the decorative border cartouches not good. So this is NOT a matter of finding gentler parameters for paper plates: they want the chroma correction OFF. MECHANISM: the plate is almost entirely pale low-chroma content on cream paper. Dropping chroma on near-white cream pushes those pixels out of a white-plus-yellow dither MIX into flat white ink, and losing the dither texture reads as losing detail. It also hurt at the other end, on the small saturated border cartouches. UNFIXED BY A, B OR C: green rings on the reference render essentially YELLOW and the plate reads generally yellower - a HUE SUBSTITUTION, the dither reaching for the wrong ink, which no pre-dither chroma curve can touch. Judged A, B, C, A.

candidate: hue f0.70 e20 vs INCUMBENT (adaptive gamma, no chroma stage), both g1.432
note: FIDELITY: B clearly - much more accurate colour, and the dark room corner reads better on B. A rendered the dress top yellower, golder than the reference: the classic low-chroma warm tone rebuilt from vivid yellow ink. COST OF B, NEW MECHANISM: loses detail; skin goes grayer; her head and the bonnet come out as indistinguishably the SAME white where the reference clearly separates them. Where two adjacent regions differ mainly in CHROMA rather than luminance, crushing chroma merges them. PREFERENCE: A, and the judge named the reason himself - I like A better, NOT closer to the reference. Judged A then B.

candidate: hue f0.70 e20 vs INCUMBENT, both g1.431
note: FIDELITY: B. Water is blue again, birds and rocks have better greys. On A the grey birds and blue water both read WAY browner than the reference - false warm colour on near-neutral content, exactly what crushing low chroma fixes. CONTRADICTS THE MAP (n12), same class, opposite verdict: the map lost because its pale content is REAL colour that crushing destroyed; the plover wins because its pale content is genuinely NEUTRAL and crushing removes false warmth. Material class alone does not predict - the discriminator looks like whether the low-chroma population is truly neutral or genuinely tinted. CROSS-CUTTING FAULT, A AND B ALIKE: the caption text under the plate is nearly invisible. Third sighting of pale detail washing out (June mantle, map whites, this caption), independent of chroma. FRAMING: far too much paper (ADR-087), on panel and reference alike - and the judge states a better crop would yield a better result but would NOT change the B selection. Framing is shared by A and B so it cancels out of the comparison: the crop re-derivation does NOT have to precede the campaign.

candidate: hue f0.70 e20 vs INCUMBENT, both g1.451
note: NEITHER IS SHIPPABLE. Judge: I would not want either of them displaying on this frame. A is super yellow with terrible detail - the constellation figure handles are unreadable. B fixes the yellow and makes the line detail WAY worse. THIS WORK CONTAINS BOTH FAILURE MODES AT ONCE: the false warm cast on pale paper that crushing chroma fixes (the plover pattern), AND the pale detail that crushing chroma destroys (the map pattern). The two demands are in direct conflict INSIDE one image, and the chroma lever only trades one for the other. That is the June-versus-Sunflowers conflict moved down a level: previously two works disagreed, here one work disagrees with itself, so no per-image parameter can resolve it either. IMPLICATION: the chroma stage is the wrong LAYER for the paper cast. Not putting yellow ink on neutral paper is an ink-selection decision, and doing it at the distance metric would leave the luminance structure that carries the linework untouched, which a pre-dither chroma cut cannot. A REGISTERED PREDICTION FAILED HERE: I predicted before the judge looked that this would behave like the map and A would win, on the theory that its pale tints are real. Wrong - it fixed the yellow like the plover AND lost detail like the map. Fourth sighting of pale detail washing out.

candidate: THREE candidates, all lost to the incumbent: B hue f0.70 e20, then D gap-normalised f0.70 floor_min 0.15. All at g1.4
note: FIDELITY: A. B lost the pale blue background almost entirely. D, the dead-zone fix, did NOT restore it - judge: same, cannot see the snowflakes, more gray than blue, looks like pencil shading. MEASURED AFTERWARDS, and it reframes the whole lever: the background blue is hue 117.6 at saturation 0.143 - genuinely FAINT and genuinely REAL. A keeps 100 pct of that chroma, B keeps 14 pct, D keeps 36 pct. D was a real improvement and still threw away most of an already faint colour, so it still reads grey. THE PREMISE IS WRONG, not the parameters. The rule assumes hue far from an ink means the colour is spurious and should be crushed. A real cyan-blue is far from every ink and still real. And the two failures run in OPPOSITE directions: June skin has source chroma 0.118 and the render ADDS false warmth (needs chroma removed); this blue has source chroma 0.143 and the render LOSES real colour to grey (needs chroma protected). Both are faint. A pre-dither chroma curve can only SUBTRACT chroma, so it can fix the first and must always worsen the second - no parameterisation escapes that, because the required correction is SIGNED and the lever points one way only. This is the empirical case for moving the correction to the distance metric, where the decision is which ink to pick rather than how much colour to remove. Sixth sighting of pale detail lost (snowflakes).
